cells.tense: You're carrying real weight right now and it isn't bending you — you've got both hands on the thing you chose, and the pressure is proving the grip rather than breaking it.
cells.ask: Hand half of one load to someone who can actually carry it, and take what they offer back without turning it into a debt.
cells.core:
You chose a direction and the choosing is holding. Hard days come and you're still pointed the same way — not because nothing's testing you, but because what you're carrying is yours and you know it. That steadiness is quiet and it's working. It's the kind that doesn't need an audience, and it's still standing after the week tried to move it.

It hasn't finished yet. Steady hands can share the load. Let one piece of what you're holding get lighter by passing half of it to someone who can carry their end, and receive what they give back as plainly as you gave it. What you've built can hold more than just you, and you're free to find out which direction it grows next.
cells.sheetLine: You picked a direction and you're still standing in it under real weight.
cells.verb: holding steady under a weight that doesn't let up
cells.place: in the part of you that picks a direction and means it

cells.tense: You're bracing for a pressure that hasn't landed yet, already holding a weight no one has handed you — living ahead of what's actually here.
cells.ask: Give one thing back that was never yours to carry and let the exchange settle where it actually belongs.
cells.core:
Enduring a hard stretch is a real capacity. But right now the bracing has gotten ahead of the thing being braced for. You're holding weight that hasn't been assigned, preparing for a test the day hasn't brought, and the holding itself has started to be the problem — more energy spent guarding against than meeting what's here.

What's weighing on you may belong on someone else's side of the scale. Hand one thing back to the person it came from, or set it down where it can be picked up by whoever it's actually for. The exchange works when both directions are real.

cells.tense: You stopped reaching for a direction and you're still standing where you stopped — the hard stretch behind you, and the hands that used to hold things open are just at your sides now.
cells.ask: Let one thing you've been holding in private be seen and named by someone — not praised, just witnessed as yours.
cells.core:
When this is going well, it's the strength that keeps carrying when no one's watching — quiet, private, yours. You get up and do the hard thing anyway, and nothing in you needs a witness for it. That's the shape of it at its best.

But right now the reaching has gone quiet. Not because you can't; because something in you stopped picking up. Pushing harder at the starved place only strains it, so that isn't the move. What refills it is having what you already gave be seen. Name one thing you've carried without telling anyone, and let someone acknowledge it out loud — the carrying becomes real when it's witnessed, and being witnessed is what hands the strength back.
cells.sheetLine: You know how to hold on, and right now you're not reaching.
cells.verb: holding steady under a weight that doesn't let up

cells.tense: You're already steering — already saying 'this, not that' with your days — and you're calling it just how things are going, as if the direction were choosing itself.
cells.ask: Say out loud, one time, that the direction you're taking is one you picked — and mean it about a stretch of your life you've been calling the situation's.
cells.core:
The steadiness is doing its work whether or not you name it. When this is going well, you know the choosing is yours — the strength comes from expecting something rather than just absorbing what arrives, and the days have a shape because you gave them one. The direction you're taking has your fingerprints all over it — the things you keep at, the things you let go of, the 'this, not that' running under everything.

It's real. It just isn't being claimed. And what feeds it is the earlier thing, the hoping, the reason all the carrying had a point. Say the direction is yours, once, out loud, about one piece of your life you've been attributing to circumstance. That naming returns the strength to its source — the source being you, deciding.
cells.sheetLine: You're already steering. You just haven't called it yours.
